indexedSections.title: The brief, and why it was wrong

value: The mandate was narrow: the intake form is bad, clean it up to reduce rework. It came from a recurring Lender Specialist complaint.

blocks.value: Half my loan requests bounce back. I redo them two or three times before Credit even looks.
The business read this as a UI problem. My first job was to test that assumption.

blocks.label: The reframe
blocks.value: The form wasn't ugly. It was collecting the Banker's information but being measured against Credit's requirements — a handoff mismatch, not a UI mismatch.

indexedSections.title: Mapping a workflow nobody owned end to end

value: Mapping the current state hit two gaps at once. No one could describe the full origination chain — each role saw its own segment and assumed the next worked fine. And there was nothing to map against: no documented IA, no personas. Everyone designed against their own mental model of the product.
So before fixing the workflow, I had to build the foundation nobody had built.

blocks.title: Build the missing source of truth

blocks.value: I interviewed lenders and domain owners across every role, embedding in check-ins and morning meetings to reach the client-facing ones, and synthesised two artefacts.

blocks.label: Impact beyond my project
blocks.value: Both became the team's source of truth — designers and POs cite them in their own reviews and roadmaps.

With the map in place I could isolate where rework happened. Instead of more interviews, I put one person from each role in a room with one anonymised deal — a real-estate investor borrowing against existing assets to buy a property — printed as a timeline on the wall.
Don't describe your job. Trace this specific deal, and put a red dot every time you had to stop and ask someone a question.

blocks.label: The deal timeline, with every stop-and-ask marked

blocks.value: The dots clustered at the same three seams every time. The most consistent: requests reaching Credit without the collateral and entity details the Banker was never asked for — the asset basis and ownership structure needed to size the facility.

items.title: NIGO
items.desc: Not-in-good-order submissions returned downstream

items.title: Restart
items.desc: Errors mid-flow forced Advisors to start over

items.title: Handoffs
items.desc: Manual back-and-forth with Credit Middle Office

blocks.value: Advisors had to already know what to do — the system rewarded institutional knowledge and penalised anyone without it.

blocks.label: The baseline
blocks.value: I audited 40 recent loan requests with Middle Office: ~60% bounced at least once, and the top two reasons matched two of the three seams.

indexedSections.title: Manufacturing an owner for an unowned problem

value: The workflow spanned four teams across USPB and IPB, each with its own regulators and roadmap. Every PO owned a slice deeply; nobody owned the seams. "Fix the intake" became a hot potato: Loan Request App called it Credit's problem, Credit called it intake's.

blocks.title: Make the problem impossible to pass along

blocks.value: The red-dot findings became a one-page Rework Map: three seams, their cost, the teams on either side. Then 45 minutes with every PO and the Credit Risk lead in one room — they had only ever met pairwise.
Quantified, in front of everyone at once, the potato became impossible to pass:
If we just told them what we needed up front, we'd stop bouncing these.

blocks.label: What that bought me
blocks.value: A de-facto sponsor by evidence, not org chart.

blocks.title: Make alignment a habit, not a meeting

blocks.value: Specialised teams spread across regions — with a pilot already live in USPB, EMEA and APAC — wouldn't stay aligned off one workshop. So I built three recurring rituals.

items.title: Design office hours
items.desc: Any PO's question, before it became a conflict.

items.title: Socialised decisions
items.desc: The why behind each decision, not just the screens.

items.title: Refinement calls
items.desc: Feasibility issues caught before anything got built wrong.

blocks.label: Why it worked
blocks.value: Alignment isn't a document — it's presence. Being in the rooms where work got scoped made me the link between siloed owners.

blocks.title: Bring design upstream of the roadmap

value: The rituals kept teams in sync but left the bigger fracture untouched: every owner could defend their slice, nobody could sequence across all of them.

Leadership called a three-day portfolio workshop at the Ohio HQ. I went as the only designer among POs, journey owners, data, architecture and risk, walking one artefact from initiative through to owner, dependency and sequence.

blocks.label: The three future-vision proposals, side by side
Why it mattered
blocks.value: The only designer at the portfolio table, I helped leadership pick a direction instead of handing design a backlog to decorate.
The boldest proposal was the AI Application Agent: auto-populate and auto-size the whole request from a chat. The business loved it. Prototype testing with two Lender Specialists hit a trust wall.
If the system sizes it and it's wrong, it's still my name on the deal. I'll just redo it by hand to be safe.

blocks.label: The trap
blocks.value: Full automation would have recreated the exact rework it was meant to remove.

I combined them. One Request, Any Deal became the backbone, killing the fork behind mis-routed intake; Collateral-First's live recalculation surfaced capacity early; the AI agent became an assist, not an autopilot — three moves for trust:

items.label: Transparency
items.title: Provenance on every value
items.desc: Every value shows its source system and as-of date.

items.label: Reversibility
items.title: The human keeps the pen
items.desc: One-click override, with a required reason.

items.label: Context flows forward
items.title: Explained, not suspicious
items.desc: Override reasons travel to Credit with the numbers.

blocks.label: A provenance chip, and the override-with-reason interaction
The rationale I'd defend in any review
blocks.value: In lending, accountability is personal. The best choice wasn't maximum automation but transparent, reversible automation — trust earned, not demanded.

NIGO — not in good order — is the firm's own term for the bounce-back rework I set out to reduce, which makes it the metric closest to the work. It's a programme-level result the redesign contributed to, alongside process and training changes.

blocks.label: What the usage mix confirms
blocks.value: Lenders (43.8%), Analysts (16.9%) and Credit Middle Office (16.3%) — the exact roles, in the exact order, the personas were built around.

blocks.label: The pilot scorecard — NIGO, adoption, and the weekly-active role mix

blocks.value: The Workspace gained coherence too: the Deal Journey Tracker now integrates the eCQ credit questionnaire and has onboarded IPB SBL and Custom deals — end-to-end visibility across the seams I mapped. The IA and personas are still the team's source of truth.

indexedSections.title: Ownership problems in a design costume

blocks.label: The takeaway
blocks.value: The hardest problems here weren't design problems — they were ownership problems in a design costume. My job was making the invisible visible until the right call was obvious.
Three moves proved repeatable beyond this project.

items.label: Move 1
items.title: When there's no source of truth, build it
items.desc: My IA and personas still anchor how the team works.

items.label: Move 2
items.title: When no one owns a problem, make it undeniable
items.desc: Then hold it through presence, not authority.

items.label: Move 3
items.title: When priority stalls, bring design upstream
items.desc: Prototypes gave leadership something to decide against.

blocks.label: What I'm still watching
blocks.value: Adoption is real but early. When Workspace dipped −10.8% week over week I didn't wave it away — seasonality or access provisioning is still an open question, and exactly the kind of signal I want instrumented rather than guessed.

What I'd do differently: wire telemetry into the two targeted seams from day one, so NIGO improvement attributes cleanly to the design change and the parked third seam has evidence ready when it comes up for prioritisation.
